newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end down on jitters before data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end down on jitters before data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower for the third straight day on Wednesday after corporate supply, rising oil prices, stronger-than-forecast consumer credit data and a news report on a private bank's rate forecast combined to push a nervous market lower.

"Corporate supply was number one," said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities, listing the reasons for the market's decline. "A couple of bid lists were rumored to hit the Street ... so there was supply."

The publication in a wire-service news story of J.P. Morgan's long-standing interest rate forecast also helped to derail a market vulnerable to jitters in front of key economic data slated for Thursday and Friday.
The market gets the December Producer Price Index (PPI) on Thursday and December employment data on Friday.

"We didn't change anything," said J.P. Morgan's James O'Sullivan of his forecast. "Someone just picked up our forecast; there's nothing new about it." O'Sullivan said he expects the Fed to raise interest rates three times in 1997 -- in March, May and August -- each time by a quarter of a point.
"The (Morgan) forecast didn't sound any different from what their basic attitude has been on the market, but the market is vulnerable," said Josh Stiles, Treasury bond strategist at I.D.E.A.

Rising oil prices and bigger than expected expansions in U.S. consumer installment debt in October and November also hurt prices, analysts said. Crude oil prices rose on Wednesday amid forecasts for colder weather.
The Fed reported that consumer credit grew by $7.4 billion in November, more than the $5.1 billion forecast.
It also revised October consumer credit growth to $6.5 billion from the $2.2 billion originally reported.

"Consumer credit should not be a number that moves the market very much, but this showed a much different picture from what people had been thinking," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "It suggests a willingness and an ability on the part of consumers to handle more debt and means that consumer spending could remain strong in early 1997."

Credit Suisse First Boston chief market strategist Matthew Alexy said the main reason for the market's decline was the unwillingness of the retail community to step in as buyers before they can define what the economy is up to.
Hedge fund selling of two- and five-year notes was another cause of the market's slide, he said.
A third reason was tightening spreads between corporate and government securities "as people reached for yield."
Alexy contradicted the notion that the market dropped because of the repetition of the J.P. Morgan forecast.

"I think everyone was trying to figure out why the market was going down so they looked at the screens and saw that and tossed it out as a reason, but I don't think that was the reason," said Alexy. "The market had already begun to move and the sellers weren't selling because of that (forecast,) because the sellers are more sophisticated than that."
The clearing away of some technical support levels in the futures market helped accentuate the selling, analysts said.
"When supports at 110-28 and 110-22 on the March T-bond were taken out, none of the locals in the pit were willing to buy and that accentuated the trade-off," said Dimick.
The bellwether 30-year U.S. Treasury bond ended the day at 95-21/32, down 20/32, yielding 6.84 percent, its highest yield since October 28, when it also ended at 6.84 percent.
Three- and six-month bill rates ended unchanged at 5.02 percent and 5.09 percent, respectively. Year bill rates rose one basis point to 5.31 percent.
Two-year notes ended at 99-17/32, down 2/32, yielding 6.00 percent. Five-year notes slid 6/32 to 99-2/32, yielding 6.35 percent. Ten-year notes fell 10/32 to 99-11/32, yielding 6.59 percent.
-- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1660
